paragraphs.text: Good afternoon, maybe I guess it's evening now, elders and sisters, but I hope you've had a wonderful day. I sure have. I've had district interviews today with two of the districts in the central zone. Got a chance to visit personally with 20 missionaries. What a great day. Great missionaries—all of you are great missionaries—but it's always a blessing for me to have these personal interviews. Love them.

All right, well, a couple of things I want to talk to you about with the gradual improvement in our quarantine. I mean, I know it's still up and down in different parts of the mission. Even though it's called a general quarantine or general community quarantine, we still have some neighborhoods that are pretty strict and we want to respect that and honor that. But I wanted to remind all the missionaries that we need to be in our proselyting clothes, dressed like missionaries, you know, in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. We need to be looking like missionaries when we go out. There was a time in the beginning of the pandemic response where we told you not to be dressed as missionaries because it was just kind of a crazy time. And we didn't know exactly what was going to happen. And so we wanted you to kind of blend in.

But now we want to get back to the mindset that we want people to know who we are. We want to be dressed like missionaries. We want to look like missionaries. And as we go out and as we go do our shopping and things like that, it's good for you to look the part. I think it'll be good for people to see you dressed like a missionary. Certainly one of the things that I've found in my life is that people tend to think about the way they dress. And if they dress sloppy, they tend to think sloppy and they tend to act sloppy. I've seen that in businesses that I've had to try to fix. And the first thing that almost always I do to get a big change in the way the culture is, is I change the way people dress at the business. And I find that it almost automatically changes the mindset of the people. Some people quit because they want to be sloppy. That's cool. They can go their own way and do their own thing. They won't go far, that's for sure. But the people who want to step it up, they find that the way they live their life is the way they are. As we have talked about so many times, what you do is who you are. And so do—is rather, how you dress is part of do. So keep that in mind.

Start making sure that you're looking sharp. All of you on your interviews are looking great. Some of you, some of you elders need to shave. There's no question about that. I mean, maybe you didn't shave when you were in high school or something, but in the mission field, it's not appropriate to be a little scruffy on the face. So I shave every day. I don't like it, but that's okay because I do it anyway. Same thing for you. Don't be growing these little baby beards on yourself. It's kind of looking silly.

Anyway, enough about that. I want to focus on another thing that I think is important. Too many missionaries are willing to just not get things done because they say the ward's not doing this or the ward's not helping there, the members are not doing this. Elders and sisters, you've got to be the game changer. You've got to be proactive. You've got to make it happen. The fact of the matter is, you're here to get the work done and you've got to be willing to, you know, really face up to situations. Right now, the members need to understand—they need to get it—that we can't find people if they don't give us referrals. We can't go get online and just, you know, put in phantom numbers and hope to find somebody. The only way we're going to find anybody to teach is with a member online referral; if we're not getting a member online referral, we're not able to do any teaching. So not only do you have to do that, you've got to get good at doing that.

And if members are not helping you... I mean, if I had a member that said, "I don't have any referrals," I'd say, "Listen, give me five names out of your Messenger. You don't even... I won't even tell them that you gave them to me. I just need to know that this is a real person and that they know a member of the church." I mean, how hard is that? I mean, the reality of it is, these members all were baptized. They all made a covenant with God to, you know, mourn with those that mourn and stand with those that are believers. And I think it's important that sometimes we have to sort of muscle up a little bit and make sure people understand that part of this thing is helping us do the work. So we're here as missionaries and we're going through the same quarantine issues and we've got challenges, but we want to do it. So don't be willing to just accept, "Oh, I don't have anybody." Push back on that.

Now it's interesting, we taught the online jiffy to the San Pablo mission and I was talking to the mission president down there and he said it's just going gangbusters. Why? Because the missionaries are pushing on it. They're asking for it. But some of you I've sensed are being a little bashful, a little shy, a little backward. And you know what? You never get anywhere if you don't go for it. So toughen up, get bold and start asking for those online referrals. You'll never be, you'll never, never, never be sad that you went out and asked for what you needed and what you wanted to do your calling. And so if people aren't willing to sort of step up and help you, well, that's their problem. It's not on you. It's on them. All right.

So enough of the tough talk. I'm sorry about that... well, I'm not sorry about it. But the fact of the matter is, I want you to know that as I've learned in my life, if you don't ask, you don't get. And you got to ask people in a way where it's unmistakable that you're asking. So no beating around the bush. And I would be just exactly that. I would go to them and say, "Hey, listen, I need to get five to 10 names off your Messenger list. We need to talk to some people. We need people to teach. We're set apart missionaries. We can't do our calling if we don't have people to teach. And, you know, before we were quarantined, we'd go out and tract for people. We can't do that right now. So we need your help, brother or sister." Anyway, and if they get upset at you, tell them to blame me. I'll take it. All right. Enough of that. Enough of that.

So let me just share another little story with you and then we'll talk about it. One day a young boy passes by a tree and sees a butterfly trying to escape out of its cocoon. There was just this little tiny opening for the butterfly, and it's trying to push its way through. And it's trying so hard, but it's not making any progress. At least that's what it looks like to the little boy. And it seemed like that the butterfly was going to give up pretty soon and then be stuck forever in that cocoon and just die there. So the little boy decides to help the butterfly, takes out his little pocket knife, cuts open the cocoon, and the butterfly immediately just pops out.

But its body was pretty weak and feeble and the wings were barely moving. And the boy started watching the butterfly and thinking, "What have I done?" hoping that the wings would spread and it would fly, but it never happened. And for the rest of its short life, that butterfly just had to kind of crawl along on the ground dragging its wings that never did spread out. And of course it didn't live very long as a result. Now, the reason that butterfly never flew—and you know the reason—it's because the boy removed the opposition and hardship that the butterfly needed. The boy wanted to help. The boy had an innocent desire to be helpful. But by removing the very obstacle that the butterfly was battling with, he caused the butterfly not to be able to gain the strength that would force the life-giving fluid out of the body into the wings and allow them to spread out and hold the butterfly in flight.

Now, life, evolution, whatever you want to call it, forced the butterfly to leave its shell in a hard way so that it would become stronger and be able to grow and develop. Now I want you to think about this in the context of you and me. If God were to allow us to live without adversity and without difficulties, how do you think we would develop? We wouldn't develop the strength necessary to achieve our greatest and most important goals and we wouldn't thrive in life for sure, and we might not even survive. We for sure wouldn't be flying. Just like that weakened butterfly, we would probably be just dragging along on the ground. So challenges are necessary to making us stronger if we will let them.

However, if we're continually complaining about our challenges, if we're continually looking at our challenges as some kind of a problem that we wish we didn't have, we won't get stronger. Challenges and hardships, adversity and opposition are like water to a ship. The ship can float on the water and use it to go where it wants to go. But if the water gets inside the ship, then the ship will sink. So remember, ships don't sink because of the water around them. Ships sink because of the water that gets in them, and people don't fail because of adversity unless they let the adversity get inside their head. And that's what we see sometimes is that people get so fixated on this challenge, that hardship, this problem, this adversity, that it gets inside their head playing an endless loop: "Why me? Why does this always happen to me? Why are we doing this? This is not what I wanted to do," and so forth and so on. And the moment you get into that mindset, the challenge stops being a benefit to you.

As you look forward, however, to meeting your challenges and overcoming your hardships, your whole mindset changes and you begin to see them as your friends. Much like a bodybuilder sees barbells and dumbbells and weights as his friends. He can't wait to get to the exercise room, throw that heavy iron around so that he can get stronger and build those muscles. He doesn't look at the barbells and dumbbells and the various weight machines, the kettlebells and all those different things—he doesn't look at those things negatively and say, "Oh, I hate those things." No, he loves those things. Why? Because he knows that through that opposition, he gets stronger.

If you want to keep building yourself, if you want to keep strengthening yourself to an ever better version of yourself, you've got to get up in the morning with this thought in mind. This is from a General Authority, passed away recently, but what a great, great man. He's a German member of the Seventy by the name of Elder F. Enzio Busche. And I'll quote this statement that he said that I was able to come across and has really affected my life, especially in some difficult days. He would get up in the morning and say this to himself: "Embrace this day with an enthusiastic welcome no matter how it looks. The covenant with God to which you are true enables you to be enlightened by him and nothing is impossible to you."

Elders and sisters, we love you. We're proud of you. We know you're trying. We know you're working hard. We know you're having some success. We want you to have more. We want you to push yourself a little harder, not because of any gain for us or even any gain for the church. We want you to push yourself harder for you, for who it's going to build you into, because life is going to be hard or easy based upon how strong you are. The stronger you are, the easier life gets. The weaker you are, the harder life gets. So why not use all of these different hardships, challenges, this adversity, this quarantine—why not use this to really create power and strength, refinement in you? Your choice. Have a good night. We'll talk to you tomorrow. Thank you.
